references.text: The midwives feared God and did not obey Pharaoh, showing the same fear of God as Pharaoh's servants displayed in Exod 9:20
Fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge, a principle illustrated by those servants who feared the word of the Lord
The Lord looks to the one who is humble and trembles at his word, the same attitude shown by the God-fearing servants
Contrasts with verse 20 by showing that Pharaoh and his servants still did not fear the Lord
Pharaoh's servants warn him that Egypt will be destroyed, demonstrating growing fear among his servants
Noah acted in reverence for God when he built the ark after God's warning, just like those servants who sought refuge at the word of the Lord
A theological parallel about God's word breaking into private households and creating fear or faith among the inhabitants.
Deuteronomy summarizes and interprets the events in Exodus as 'awesome signs,' adding theological depth to the servants' reaction.
Clear theological contrast: Fear of human opinion (Gideon) versus fear of the Lord's word that leads to salvation.
Theological progression: From individual fear among some Egyptians (Exod 9) to collective faith and fear among the Israelites after the judgments were fulfilled (Exod 14).
